claims.text: The sub-10 nm equiatomic Au-Co-Cu-Ni-Pt nanoparticles initially form a disordered solid solution.
Below 10 nm, the sluggish-diffusion effect is kinetically suppressed.
Surface-energy minimization and vacancy-mediated surface diffusion dominate the structural evolution of sub-10 nm particles.
The concentration of surface vacancies scales inversely with particle radius.
Surface diffusion pathways override constraints imposed by bulk lattice diffusion in these nanoparticles.
Bulk high-entropy alloys can exhibit sluggish diffusion associated with lattice distortion and chemical complexity.
Surface diffusion coefficients in sub-10 nm particles exceed bulk diffusion coefficients by orders of magnitude.
The high curvature of smaller particles gives them a higher chemical potential than larger particles.
Surface-mediated mass transport transfers material from smaller particles to larger particles, producing Ostwald ripening.
Surface diffusion drives shape relaxation toward lower-surface-area spherical or faceted shapes.
Surface-driven transport bypasses stabilization attributed to configurational entropy.
Heating to 1000 K will cause rapid loss of the smallest particles through evaporation or dissolution into larger particles.
Heating will significantly increase the average particle size.
The particles will not retain their initial equiatomic elemental distribution during heating.
The initially single-phase particles will undergo phase separation or elemental segregation driven by surface-energy minimization.
High configurational entropy can stabilize a single-phase state in an equimolar five-component material.
Bulk TiCoCrFeMn exhibits substantial long-term structural stability and limited grain growth during high-temperature annealing.
The cited TiCoCrFeMn evidence demonstrates a single-phase material with no phase separation.
For particles larger than 50 nm, bulk sluggish diffusion should dominate and produce high-entropy-theory stability.
